title: AGI in 2030: What's Your School's Value Proposition in the Age of AGI?
author: Bauschard, Stefan
summary: Stefan Bauschard begins from Demis Hassabis's prediction of AGI by 2030 under a strict definition: a system that can exhibit all cognitive capabilities humans can, including the highest levels of creativity and the ability to generate novel hypotheses rather than solve given problems. The article notes that AGI timelines from major labs are compressing, not expanding, and that even skeptics like Gary Marcus push back only to 'another 10 years, not never.' The decisive point for education is that the capabilities being produced en route to AGI are already transforming what cognitive labor commands a wage. The agricultural-to-industrial analogy is applied honestly: just as the Prussian school model evolved to produce factory workers, today's school model was optimized for stable cognitive labor in offices and labs—exactly the economy AI is disrupting first. The article does not claim to have the new school model but insists the old value proposition (credentials + cognitive skills = good job) is being invalidated in real time, and asks school leaders to sit with the harder questions: What can humans do that machines genuinely cannot? What is school for when the labor market argument weakens?
points: Hassabis's AGI definition is substantially harder than 'outperforms humans on economically valuable work.' A system that can exhibit all cognitive capabilities humans can—including proposing new scientific questions rather than solving existing ones—has never moved its goalposts despite market pressure to declare victory early. That discipline makes his 2030 prediction more, not less, credible as a directional signal.

The capabilities produced en route to AGI are already transformative regardless of whether the North Star is reached. Drug discovery timelines collapsing from a decade to months, 1000x engineer productivity gains, and AI doing real legal research and financial analysis—these are happening now and are eliminating the entry-level rungs of cognitive professions that school credentials once certified.

Schools' current value proposition rests on four assumptions AI is actively dismantling: that cognitive output is scarce and valuable; that credentials reliably signal capability; that curriculum change can roughly match labor market change; and that the tasks schools optimize for (recall, structured writing, procedural problem-solving) are the ones the economy will keep paying for.

The honest version of the agricultural analogy does not claim to know what comes next. It only insists that the transition is analogous in scale and that schools which wait until AGI arrives to rethink their purpose will have waited too long. The new value proposition must answer what AI cannot: what it means to develop judgment, agency, ethics, and the capacity to act well under genuine uncertainty.
quotes: Schools should be paying attention — because the ground under their value proposition is shifting the way it shifted when we left the farms.

Even if you discount the lab CEOs by 50% on the assumption that they are talking their book, you still end up with a transformative capability arriving sometime in the early-to-mid 2030s — well within the working life of every student.

Cognitive output is being commoditized in real time. Credentials that signaled 'this person can synthesize sources and write a coherent argument' no longer reliably signal that, because the AI can do it for the student or instead of the student.

If your school's value proposition is still 'we will help your child accumulate the cognitive skills and credentials that lead to a good job,' you are running on borrowed time. The cognitive skills are being commoditized. The credential signal is weakening. The good job is being restructured.
The North Star is moving. Schools that wait until it arrives will have waited too long.
